Jesus Prayer and recollection of God

Worship and practice · Prayer

Jesus Prayer and recollection of God

4 sectionsNot completed
Notes

The Jesus Prayer is a short prayer addressed to Jesus Christ for mercy. The other selections describe St. Cassian’s teaching about continual recollection of God using a Psalm verse; these are distinct source texts.[1][2]

What is expressed in the Jesus Prayer?[1]

The supplied wording addresses Jesus as Lord and Son of God and asks for mercy. Its reference to the speaker as a sinner expresses repentance within the prayer’s own published text.[1]

Read original passage

Jesus Prayer

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me a sinner.

Which short prayer does St. Cassian discuss?[2]

St. Cassian’s passage identifies a Psalm verse asking for God’s saving help as a means of recollection. Recollection here means keeping God in mind. The text connects the verse with many different circumstances; it does not identify this verse as the wording of the Jesus Prayer.[2]

Read original passage

Psalm verse in Cassian

And so for keeping up continual recollection of God this pious formula is to be ever set before you. "O God, make speed to save me: O Lord, make haste to help me," [1673] for this verse has not unreasonably been picked out from the whole of Scripture for this purpose. For it embraces all the feelings which can be implanted in human nature, and can be fitly and satisfactorily adapted to every condition, and all assaults.

How does St. Cassian describe continual recollection?[2]

St. Cassian describes the repeated remembrance of the Psalm verse across work, travel, difficulty, prosperity and rest. His account relates this persistence to purification and prayer.[2]

Read original passage

Recollection of God

We must then ceaselessly and continuously pour forth the prayer of this verse, in adversity that we may be delivered, in prosperity that we may be preserved and not puffed up. Let the thought of this verse, I tell you, be conned over in your breast without ceasing. Whatever work you are doing, or office you are holding, or journey you are going, do not cease to chant this. When you are going to bed, or eating, and in the last necessities of nature, think on this. This thought in your heart maybe to you a saving formula, and not only keep you unharmed by all attacks of devils, but also purify you from all faults and earthly stains, and lead you to that invisible and celestial contemplation, and carry you on to that ineffable glow of prayer, of which so few have any experience. Let sleep come upon you still considering this verse, till having been moulded by the constant use of it, you grow accustomed to repeat it even in your sleep.

The Jesus Prayer in an OCA resource[1]

The linked OCA article concerns the Jesus Prayer. It supplies further context while keeping that prayer distinct from St. Cassian’s Psalm-based teaching.[1]
